inferred: The size of work that has not started yet, matched by shape against similar past sessions (H1), then turned into a probability of overrunning the window. Two stacked guesses: that a prompt's text predicts its duration, and that a past session was 'similar'.
falsePositiveCost: 'You cannot finish this' defers a job the user could have completed. They either sit out a two-hour reset for nothing or fragment a task that wanted one continuous run, which is the cost the whole usage cluster exists to avoid.
falseNegativeCost: 'You are fine, start it' and then the wall lands mid-job. This is A1's headline pain, now delivered with the tool's blessing, and the user has stopped checking their status line because Cargento said it would tell them. Strictly worse than shipping nothing.

inferred: That nothing needs you for N minutes. Three low-confidence inputs ANDed into one positive assurance: nothing is currently blocked (B1/B2, heuristic on eight of nine harnesses), nothing will block within N minutes (D3's ETAs), and nothing is silently wedged (C2). The all-clear is the product; the components are the weakest signals on the board.
falsePositiveCost: Withholding the all-clear when the user was in fact free costs them only the nicety. They keep checking the board, which is exactly today's behaviour. Near zero, and freely dismissible.
falseNegativeCost: The user leaves the desk on the tool's word. A gate rots for 40 minutes, or a wedged agent eats the window while nobody is watching. One wrong all-clear teaches the user that the product lies, and it takes D6, D4 and H2 down with it because they share the same voice. Unrecoverable in trust terms.

inferred: Semantic equivalence between tracked task rows and the actual diff. Requires judging whether a differently-worded implementation satisfies a task, which is model work, and the no-model-summarization promise means it has to be a local model with correspondingly weak judgement.
falsePositiveCost: 'Scope drift detected' when the diff simply implements the task in different words sends the user to re-read a large diff by hand. That is the single most expensive review action available, spent on nothing, and after two of them nobody opens the panel again.
falseNegativeCost: 'Plan matches work' when a task was silently skipped or an extra one snuck in. The user ships believing the plan was followed. This is the exact case the feature exists for, so a miss is not a gap in coverage, it is the feature failing at its only job.

inferred: Intent. Whether an agent that is still emitting is productive or wedged, read off behavioural traces: repeated identical tool calls, the same file rewritten, a test re-run loop, recurring error strings. The problem is that those patterns are also what correct work looks like, and the genuinely novel wedges (an agent spiralling into longer plans, quietly redefining the task, waiting on a call that never returns) emit no repetition at all.
falsePositiveCost: You interrupt a working agent. You lose its plan and context, possibly kill an expensive turn near completion, and pay a restart. Note the response to 'stuck' is intervention, not dismissal, so the FP is not free the way a badge is. Repeated FPs also train the user to ignore the signal, which silently converts the detector into a false-negative machine and hollows out D5 and D7.
falseNegativeCost: A wedged agent runs two hours and burns the whole 5h window, the most expensive failure mode on the board, while the user is away because the walk-away promise rests on this item. Silent, expensive, and it arrives in one trust-destroying event rather than gradually.

inferred: Stake, from proxies nobody validated: a repo name, a branch name, the presence of a deploy step. Each proxy fails routinely. `main` in a scratch repo, a feature branch that deploys to prod, a repo called sandbox that holds the production config.
falsePositiveCost: Everything reads as high stakes and the field stops carrying information. The sort it feeds (D7) then ranks by noise, which is worse than ranking by recency because recency is at least honest about what it is.
falseNegativeCost: Production work labelled low stakes. The user deprioritizes review on the one session that could break something, with the tool endorsing the choice. This is the clearest item on the board where a wrong inference leaves the user worse off than no feature, and the item's own note already says so.

inferred: Two things, stacked. First the intended scope, which outside Spacedock has no source at all and must be guessed from the opening prompt. Then whether current activity violates it, when touching a neighbouring file, fixing a test or updating an import is routinely legitimate inside any real task.
falsePositiveCost: Accusing a correct agent of going off-rail. The user interrupts good work, and worse, learns to distrust drift warnings, which is the one class where a single true positive is worth a great deal (an agent quietly rewriting CI config). It also makes the user doubt instructions that were fine.
falseNegativeCost: The agent rewrites forty files nobody asked for and it surfaces at review time. Expensive, but recoverable: the diff still exists and git still has the before state, which is why this sits below C2 rather than beside it.

inferred: Forward consumption rate, extrapolated from recent token or request throughput to a time-of-exhaustion. The series is non-stationary and bursty: an agent that just went idle carries a stale high rate, a compaction or a large file read spikes it, and the burn over the next hour depends mostly on what the user chooses to launch next, which is not in the data at all.
falsePositiveCost: 'Wall in 22 minutes' when it is two hours away. The user pauses work they could have finished, or triggers E7's hand-off ritual early and fragments a task. Bounded and self-correcting, because the wall visibly fails to arrive.
falseNegativeCost: 'Plenty left' and the user starts the long job. Force-paused mid-job, restart by hand after the reset. That is the single most-cited pain on this board, and A5's entire delta over A1 is the projection, so a wrong projection means the user paid DEC-1's promise amendment for a number that misled them.

inferred: A binary verdict, 'safe to start', composed from A5's projection plus a threshold nobody can set correctly because the tool does not know how large the job the user is about to start is. Collapsing to one bit also discards the nuance that would let the user sanity-check the call.
falsePositiveCost: A red light when capacity was fine. The user waits two hours or downshifts to a weaker model for nothing, and unlike A5 they cannot see the working to argue with it.
falseNegativeCost: A green light and then the wall. Worse than A5's miss, because the user delegated the judgement entirely, which was the point of collapsing it into a light. A green light that lied once is not trusted again, and then the whole usage cluster is decoration.

inferred: Remaining time for a turn whose remaining work is unknown. There is no progress denominator: the agent does not know how many tool calls are left, so the ETA is elapsed-time extrapolation over a heavy-tailed distribution where most turns are short and a few are twenty times longer. Shipped and labelled naive, so this risk is realized rather than hypothetical.
falsePositiveCost: Says two minutes, takes twenty. The user waits, or comes back and it is still running. That is precisely the keep-coming-back behaviour the item exists to stop, so a wrong ETA delivers negative value against its own stated outcome.
falseNegativeCost: Says twenty minutes, finishes in two. The user leaves and a finished or blocked session sits dead for eighteen minutes. On a blocked session the whole downstream pipeline stalls on a number that was optimistically wrong.

inferred: That local output-token share equals share of the quota pool. It does not: quota consumption is weighted across input, cache and output, is per-model, is partly request-count based, and includes consumers Cargento cannot see at all (Claude Desktop, web, another machine on the same account). The ranking is a proxy dressed as an attribution.
falsePositiveCost: Unusually expensive for this board, because the action attached is 'kill that one'. You terminate an innocent session and lose its in-flight work while the actual consumer keeps burning. A destructive FP, not a dismissible one.
falseNegativeCost: You cannot identify the consumer, so you kill everything or nothing. That is today's status quo, so the miss costs no new harm.

inferred: Blocked-on-human state on eight harnesses that expose no such signal. Where typed events exist (Copilot) it is close to a read; where none exist (Pi, per the briefing) it is pattern matching on scrollback and session files across eight undocumented, independently version-drifting surfaces. The 'differentiated' score is an average over eight quite different detection problems.
falsePositiveCost: Pings on sessions that are not blocked. The badge becomes noise, and because it is the same badge as B1, the FP rate on the eight contaminates the one harness where the signal is hook-grade and trustworthy.
falseNegativeCost: The promise is 'not blocked, anywhere'. A missed gate sits for hours, and the deeper harm is induced reliance: the user stopped cycling tabs because Cargento said it would tell them. They are now less likely to catch a gate than before installing it.

inferred: That N past interactions were 'the same thing'. That is semantic clustering of prompts and decisions, which needs judgement the no-model promise forbids, on top of a history store (H1) that does not exist yet.
falsePositiveCost: The weak half is a spurious 'make this a skill' suggestion, which is cheap noise. The strong half is not: the item's stated outcome is taking the user out of a decision. Generalizing from a pattern that was not real removes the human from a decision class that needed them, and the resulting auto-approvals are invisible until one is wrong.
falseNegativeCost: No suggestion appears and the user keeps answering the same question by hand. That is today, so the miss costs nothing new.

inferred: Every bucket in 'three finished, one needs you, one stuck' is a separate detector: E2's completion inference, B1/B2's needs-input, C2's wedge verdict. The digest also implies completeness, and a re-entry summary that omits a session reads as an all-clear about that session.
falsePositiveCost: A session listed as finished that actually died mid-way (E3). The user does not go look, and the half-done work is quietly abandoned with the digest's blessing.
falseNegativeCost: A session omitted, and the user re-enters believing they are caught up. The whole point of the item is to replace the full re-scan, so an incomplete digest removes the safety net it substituted for.

inferred: Hours of human attention. Cargento can see when a gate opened and when it closed, but not whether the user was attending in between, so wall-clock gaps include lunch and sleep. The headline number is systematically inflated, or if measured from activity, systematically deflated.
falsePositiveCost: This is explicitly the one artifact a user would show their manager. An inflated 'hours spent answering agents' figure is load-bearing in a real conversation about headcount or delegation, and being caught out with a number the tool made up is worse than having no number.
falseNegativeCost: The case for delegating never gets made and behaviour does not change. That is today, so no new harm.

inferred: The workflow to generate. Turning an observed session pattern into stages, entities and a first-officer contract worth accepting is a semantic judgement, and it is a write, not a readout.
falsePositiveCost: A workflow that does not fit the work. The user changes their role, runs their project through the generated scaffolding, hits friction, and reverts, having paid the setup cost twice. The item is positioned as the moment the user's role changes, so a bad first attempt poisons the whole Spacedock on-ramp.
falseNegativeCost: No promotion offered, and the user keeps hand-orchestrating. That is today.

inferred: The minimum over D3's per-turn ETAs, presented as one clock time. The claim is genuinely weaker than D5's, but the behaviour it induces is not: hand someone a single time to come back and they will leave the desk, so in practice it functions as an all-clear it never states. That gap is where the risk was banked as differentiation.
falsePositiveCost: 3:40 arrives and there is nothing to do. One wasted return trip, which is what happens today anyway.
falseNegativeCost: Something wanted the user at 3:05 and the board said 3:40. A gate rots for thirty-five minutes. Partly backstopped by D4's notifications, but only if the user is at the machine (H2's gap) and only if the block was detected at all (B2's gap), so the backstop is thinnest on exactly the harnesses where the ETA is weakest.

inferred: That the wall is coming, at full inheritance from A5's projection, plus the choice of the moment to fire. The hand-off text itself is the agent's own work, not Cargento's inference, which is what keeps this below A5.
falsePositiveCost: Self-defeating: a spurious fire interrupts a working agent to write a summary, spending quota and breaking a turn to prepare for a wall that is not coming. The mitigation consumes the resource it exists to protect.
falseNegativeCost: It does not fire and the wall lands with no hand-off. That is today, and the user still has the manual ritual they invented, so the miss costs nothing new. This asymmetry is unusually favourable and is the reason to build it.

inferred: Which prompts count as reviews. The item's own needs line admits it: 'a rule for deciding'. Without a model that is keyword matching on prompt text.
falsePositiveCost: An urgent inline question gets misfiled as a Spacedock gate and deferred into a batch. The agent then sits blocked longer than if nothing had routed it, so a false positive here produces a false-negative-shaped harm.
falseNegativeCost: The prompt stays inline and is answered where it was raised. Status quo, no loss.

inferred: Which tool calls were irreversible. Literal command shapes (`git push --force`, `DROP TABLE`) are read, not inferred, and that is the honest core. The inference is the boundary: `rm -rf` in a scratch dir, a reset --hard on a branch nobody wanted, a shell one-liner that is arbitrarily destructive.
falsePositiveCost: Alarm about a scoped, safe action (dropping a temp table every test run) trains the user to skim exactly the log that needs to be trusted. It can also provoke a panicked recovery that is itself destructive, force-pushing back over good work.
falseNegativeCost: A genuinely irreversible action goes unlogged and surfaces days later. Note the counterfactual is generous: today there is no log at all, so an omission leaves the user where they already were, unless the panel is framed as complete, in which case an empty list is a false all-clear.

inferred: Comparability. Each vendor's own number is a read, but normalizing nine different quota semantics (different windows, units, reset behaviour, request-versus-token accounting) into 'Claude 95%, Codex 10%' is inference. The briefing also says quota display is absent on most harnesses, so for those the figure has to be reconstructed from observed consumption rather than read.
falsePositiveCost: You migrate a long job to a harness that is not actually the roomier one, paying the whole context-transfer cost for nothing and arriving at a second wall.
falseNegativeCost: You do not migrate when you could have, and wait out a reset. That is today's behaviour, so the miss is a missed win rather than a new loss.

inferred: Only the leap from 'repeating' to 'unproductive'. The repetition itself is counted from transcript text, which makes this the most nearly-factual detector in the C cluster and the reason it is the shippable slice of C2.
falsePositiveCost: Fires on legitimate iteration, and this user's own conventions make that common: red-green TDD means a test failing five times in a row is correct practice, flaky integration tests get retried on purpose, a lint burndown loop is a loop by design. On a naive threshold the FP rate in this workflow is high.
falseNegativeCost: An expensive loop keeps running and a 5h window goes. Bounded by the window, and the user is no worse off than today because nothing told them they were safe. Materially cheaper than C2's miss, which is inherited by D5's all-clear.

inferred: Where SessionEnd arrives (Claude) this is a read. Elsewhere it is inference from process liveness, last-write time and the absence of a clean ending. PID liveness is a checkable fact, which rescues most of the confidence; the guessy part is separating crashed from exited-cleanly-after-finishing from alive-but-silent.
falsePositiveCost: Unusually costly. 'Died, restart it' on a session that actually finished means duplicate work and possibly duplicate side effects: a second PR, a second deploy, a second migration. One of the few FPs on this board that can do real external damage.
falseNegativeCost: It reads as Idle, indistinguishable from done, and the user waits on something that is never coming back. That is the harm the item names, and it is today's behaviour, so the miss costs no new harm beyond the wait.

inferred: Not much is inferred about the world, but the target is: which prompt is live, in which session, and which option maps to which keystroke. Value depends on that identification being right rather than on any behavioural heuristic.
falsePositiveCost: A misrouted answer is a write into a live agent. Approving the wrong session's pending tool call can authorize something destructive, which is a categorically different failure from a wrong badge and the reason this needs confirmation surfaces rather than one-click answering.
falseNegativeCost: The answer does not land and the user walks to the tab, which is what they do today. Near zero.

inferred: That an idle session finished, rather than stopped. 'Completion' has no marker on most harnesses: a turn that ended is not a task that finished, so a context limit, a refusal, or a crash (E3) all read as done.
falsePositiveCost: You are told there is finished work waiting, open it, and find a half-done job or an unanswered question. A wasted trip, and the tab holds ground truth so it self-corrects immediately.
falseNegativeCost: Finished work stays unread, which is precisely today's status quo. The downside of a miss is no improvement rather than a new harm, and that asymmetry is why this carries a much smaller discount than its neighbours in the differentiated corner.

inferred: Two claims of very different quality. Grouping by shared repo and overlapping time is near-read and reliable. That the group constitutes a workflow worth proposing is a judgement with no source.
falsePositiveCost: A recurring nag to formalize four unrelated sessions that merely share a monorepo. Dismissible individually, but in a monorepo it fires constantly, and a suggestion that is wrong every day is uninstall-grade.
falseNegativeCost: No suggestion, and the user keeps hand-orchestrating. Status quo.

inferred: Only that current output rate predicts near-term consumption, and that output tokens proxy quota cost well enough to rank. A much weaker claim than A7's attribution, and the user can watch the rate move and check it.
falsePositiveCost: You stop a session that was about to finish anyway. Real but modest, and visible to the user before they act.
falseNegativeCost: The ranking misleads and you stop the wrong one, which is today's coin flip. No new harm.

inferred: Inside Spacedock the goal is read from entity state. Outside it, the goal is inferred from the opening prompt, which is a label rather than a verdict, so a wrong one misdescribes rather than misdirects.
falsePositiveCost: A mislabelled goal means you recognise a session wrongly and open the wrong one. Cheap, immediate, self-correcting.
falseNegativeCost: No goal shown, which is today. Cheap.

inferred: A priority ordering, which is a value judgement over sessions. Composed from read state plus B6's wait time, and if it consumes D8's stakes it inherits that item's low-confidence proxies wholesale.
falsePositiveCost: The row that mattered is ranked third. Small, because nothing is hidden and the full list is still the safety net.
falseNegativeCost: Same: mis-ranked but still present. The discount stays low only while the sort shows everything. The moment it collapses or hides rows, it becomes a filter rather than an order, and it should be re-priced near D5.

inferred: The transport itself infers nothing. The risk is multiplicative: a push off the machine carries whatever D5, D6, C2 and B2 concluded, and a phone buzz cannot be dismissed as cheaply as a dashboard badge, while a push that never arrives is a total failure because the user is by definition not looking.
falsePositiveCost: A wrong push while the user is at dinner. Higher unit cost than any in-app FP, which is why this channel needs a precision-first gate: push only hook-grade signals such as Claude's needs-input, never an inferred wedge or an all-clear.
falseNegativeCost: The signal never reaches them. Every other item's walk-away promise silently fails at the exact moment it was supposed to pay off.

inferred: Nothing new, but the clock starts at whatever moment B1/B2 decided the session became blocked. The duration is exactly as good as that timestamp.
falsePositiveCost: An overstated wait promotes a session that only just blocked. Mild mis-triage.
falseNegativeCost: An understated wait, from a badge that flipped late, hides a gate that has actually been rotting for an hour. That is the direction that matters, and on the eight non-Claude harnesses it is the likely one.

inferred: For Claude, the Notification hook makes this close to a read; the transcript path is the heuristic half, deciding whether an assistant turn is a question awaiting the human or rhetorical mid-plan text.
falsePositiveCost: You context-switch to a session that did not need you. Attention cost, and repeated it is fatigue on Cargento's single best signal.
falseNegativeCost: A gate sits unanswered while the user believes they are free. This is the flagship failure, but hooks plus a shipped, exercised implementation keep it rare on Claude specifically.

inferred: The stage is read from Spacedock state files, and the tripwire condition is declared by the user, so almost nothing is inferred. The residual risk is staleness: state advances only when a worker writes it, so a tripwire evaluates against a possibly old position.
falsePositiveCost: A tripwire fires on a stage the workflow has already left. The user investigates a line that was crossed and un-crossed. Annoying, cheap.
falseNegativeCost: The line is crossed and nothing fires because the state file had not been written yet. The user declared a condition and it silently did not hold, which is worse than not offering tripwires, so the staleness window needs stating in the UI.

inferred: Nothing of its own. It is a transport over B1/B2's state transitions and inherits their error rates without adding inference.
falsePositiveCost: A spurious pop for a state change that did not happen. Dismissible, and already shipped without complaint on Claude.
falseNegativeCost: A transition that fires no notification, so the user goes on polling the dashboard, which is the behaviour the item removes. Bounded because the board still shows the state.

inferred: The git fact is a read, not an inference; the interpretation is inferred, namely that uncommitted means unfinished and at risk. Deliberate scratch edits, generated files and untracked build output all present as dirt.
falsePositiveCost: Nagging about intentional dirt. The flag gets ignored, and then the one real loss slips past it.
falseNegativeCost: Real uncommitted work is not flagged and evaporates in a worktree nobody revisited, which the item correctly calls the way agent work actually gets lost. Low probability once the git read exists, because the underlying signal is a fact.

inferred: Whether an unmerged branch or an open PR was 'left behind' rather than deliberately in flight. The branch and PR state themselves are read from git and the GitHub API.
falsePositiveCost: A long-lived intentional branch nagged as abandoned. Trivial, dismissible.
falseNegativeCost: An abandoned branch stays invisible. That is today, and the work is still in git, so nothing is destroyed.

inferred: Almost nothing. The question text and its options are already parsed to raise B1's flag; the inference is only which block is the live one and how to truncate it. On the eight non-Claude harnesses there is nothing to parse, so the honest output there is blank rather than a guess.
falsePositiveCost: A stale or wrong question shown. The user answers the wrong thing, or walks to the tab anyway, and the tab is ground truth so it corrects within seconds.
falseNegativeCost: The row says nothing and the user makes the trip. Status quo.

inferred: The mapping from a session to an OS window, tab or tmux pane. Ambiguous when two panes share a cwd, or when a session has been reattached elsewhere.
falsePositiveCost: Focuses the wrong pane. The user notices instantly and cycles by hand. Close to zero.
falseNegativeCost: Focus fails and the user hunts across tabs, which is today's behaviour.

inferred: Nothing of its own. The queue's ordering is arithmetic and its completeness is B1/B2's problem, not this item's.
falsePositiveCost: One extra row to dismiss inside a list the user is already reading top to bottom.
falseNegativeCost: A missing row, but the omission belongs to the upstream detector and should be priced there rather than twice.

inferred: Session discovery is a read of known store paths. The residual risk is completeness rather than inference: an unrecognised harness, a relocated store, a session started before the collector knew about it.
falsePositiveCost: A phantom or duplicated row. Confusing for a moment, cheap to resolve.
falseNegativeCost: A silently missing session. 'Every session, one screen' implies completeness, so an absent row is a small false all-clear about the user's own fleet, and it propagates into D5, D6 and D10, all of which quantify over whatever D1 found.

inferred: A title, derived from the first prompt or the harness's own session name. A label, not a verdict.
falsePositiveCost: A misleading one-liner sends the user into the wrong pane. One wasted click.
falseNegativeCost: An unhelpful label and they cycle tabs, which is today.

inferred: Nothing, if the spend fields arrive in A1's payload. If computed instead, it is arithmetic over a pricing table, so the failure mode is stale prices or unmodelled cache discounts rather than a behavioural guess.
falsePositiveCost: An overstated figure makes a cheap run look expensive and may push the user off a model unnecessarily.
falseNegativeCost: An understated figure. Matters for API-key and team accounts, and barely at all for the subscription user this board models.

inferred: Only the rule that two sessions in one repo risk colliding. The cwds themselves are read. Misses exist (same repo reached via worktree or symlink, or collision through a shared port or database rather than files) but they are cheap.
falsePositiveCost: Two agents flagged who were on separate worktrees or one only reading. A warning the user dismisses in a second.
falseNegativeCost: The collision happens and two agents fight over a file. Expensive, but identical to today, and the build cost is near zero so the expected value survives a mediocre hit rate.

inferred: Nothing in the schedule itself, which is a user setting and a clock. The one inherited risk is the carve-out: 'suppress everything except your-call' relies on B1/B2 classifying your-call correctly.
falsePositiveCost: Something non-urgent breaks through quiet hours, which defeats the point of the block but costs one interruption.
falseNegativeCost: A genuine your-call gate is suppressed because it was not classified as one. The user asked for protection and got silence instead, so the exception list should fail open rather than closed.

inferred: Nothing yet, because the item is a feasibility question. Either a local artifact exists and this becomes a read, or none exists and there is nothing to infer from, in which case it does not ship. Answer the question before pricing it.
falsePositiveCost: Showing a hosted session's state from a stale or partial artifact would misreport a session the user cannot see any other way, so there is no cross-check.
falseNegativeCost: Hosted sessions stay invisible, which is today.

inferred: Nothing inferred; transport and identity. Same staleness risk as F4, multiplied by the number of machines and by clock skew between them.
falsePositiveCost: A machine that dropped off shows stale rows and the user acts on a snapshot that has moved.
falseNegativeCost: A machine's sessions never appear and the fleet view is quietly partial.

inferred: Versions are read. 'Health' is the mildly inferred part: whether a harness that has not been seen recently is broken or merely unused.
falsePositiveCost: A harness reported unhealthy when it was simply idle. The user goes looking for a problem that is not there.
falseNegativeCost: A genuinely broken harness reported fine, and the user wonders why no sessions appear. Cheap to diagnose by hand.

inferred: Only the two-hour threshold, which is a stated convention over a read timestamp. The docs already gloss the ambiguity honestly rather than resolving it by guessing.
falsePositiveCost: A deliberately parked session flagged stale. Dismissible.
falseNegativeCost: A session abandoned at one hour fifty-five is not flagged. Trivial.

inferred: Nothing inferred; remote state is read. The residual is staleness, where a lost connection makes a live cloud session present as idle.
falsePositiveCost: A cloud session shown as running when it has stopped. The user waits on it.
falseNegativeCost: A cloud session shown as idle when it is working, which invites a duplicate launch.

inferred: Nothing. The rate is measured from tokens actually observed. Its weakness is that a rate without a ceiling supports no decision, which is an impact problem, not a detector problem.
falsePositiveCost: A smoothing artefact makes a spike look like a trend. Nobody acts on it, because there is no action attached.
falseNegativeCost: A real burst is smoothed away. Same: no decision was resting on it.

inferred: Nothing beyond the threshold that defines 'active', which is a stated convention rather than a guess.
falsePositiveCost: The count is off by one. No decision hangs on it.
falseNegativeCost: Same. Furniture.

inferred: Nothing. The model is named in the transcript. The one risk is staleness after a mid-session model switch.
falsePositiveCost: A stale model label sends the user to change a model that was already changed, or makes them think cheap work is on Opus when it is not.
falseNegativeCost: A stale label hides expensive work on the expensive model, which removes the control surface A3 needs to be actionable.

inferred: Nothing. five_hour.utilization and resets_at are read fields. The open question is DEC-1's promise amendment, not accuracy. The only accuracy risk is cache staleness across a reset boundary.
falsePositiveCost: A stale reading shows less headroom than exists and the user waits unnecessarily.
falseNegativeCost: A stale reading shows more headroom than exists and the user hits the wall believing they were clear. Argues for showing the fetch timestamp rather than the number alone.

inferred: Nothing. Read from the same payload as A1, with the same cache-staleness caveat and a longer window that makes staleness matter less.
falsePositiveCost: Understated headroom defers a big job by a day.
falseNegativeCost: Overstated headroom starts a big job on Thursday that cannot finish.

inferred: Nothing. The per-model fields sit alongside A1's. Actionability depends on joining to G3 to know which session is on which model, but that is also a read.
falsePositiveCost: A wrong per-model figure prompts a model switch that was not needed, costing a little quality for nothing.
falseNegativeCost: A wrong figure hides that the Opus sub-limit is nearly gone, and the one-keystroke remedy is missed.

inferred: Nothing. A user action written to local state and read back. No heuristic can be wrong here, provided dismissals are never auto-expired or auto-reapplied by a rule.
falsePositiveCost: None, unless a dismissal is dropped, in which case a cleared row reappears.
falseNegativeCost: None, unless a dismissal outlives the thing it dismissed and hides a session that became live again. That is the one place to avoid being clever.

inferred: Nothing. Counts over H1's record. There is no decision attached, so there is no asymmetry to price.
falsePositiveCost: A wrong streak. Nobody acts on it.
falseNegativeCost: A missing session in the count. Same.

inferred: Nothing. Appending observed events. Every inference the history enables (A6, D10, F2, F3) is priced on those items, not here. The risk this item carries is retention and trust, which is a different axis.
falsePositiveCost: None from a detector. A recording error would corrupt downstream items rather than mislead directly.
falseNegativeCost: A gap in the record silently weakens A6, D10, F2 and F3 without any of them knowing they are reasoning over a hole, so the store should record its own coverage gaps.
